summary: The paper studies a one-pass filter that drops each training sample whose out-of-fold logistic regression prediction disagrees with its given label, then refits. On digits and breast cancer, with clean labels and two rates of symmetric noise over five seeds, the refit model beats unfiltered logistic regression in all noisy runs but one, drops mostly mislabeled samples under noise and loses little on clean labels, with weak recovery on breast cancer at the higher rate. The authors claim no new method, and they run no random-drop, oracle or competing noisy-label filtering baseline.
strengths: The claims are mostly scoped to what was run. The weak cases are stated openly (breast cancer at both noise rates, discarded correct samples, the remaining gap to clean labels), and the paper says that the MLP gap does not isolate filtering.

The method is simple and clearly specified. One equation gives the keep rule, standardization is refit inside every fold and again before the final fit, test labels stay clean, and K and C are fixed rather than tuned.
The comparison is paired on shared splits and noisy labels, and Fig. 2 shows every per-seed difference, so the one unfavorable noisy run is visible.
The paper measures what is removed (drop fraction, precision and recall against the known flips) and the clean-label cost, not only test accuracy.

Tables 1 and 2 and Fig. 2 are clean and easy to read, bold marks the best mean even when it is not the proposed method, and Fig. 1a explains the pipeline without the text, including that a correct sample can be dropped.

weaknesses.issue: The experiments cannot show that the gain comes from choosing the right samples, or that the filter is preferable to any other cheap remedy. The only comparison that isolates filtering is against unfiltered logistic regression at a fixed C = 1. There is no random-drop or oracle control, no thresholded confident learning or voting filter, and no check of whether stronger regularization alone narrows the gap. The MLP does not fill this role. The missing controls surface only in the last paragraph, after the abstract and contributions have already framed the gain as accuracy 'won back'.
weaknesses.where: Abstract; Sec. 1, third contribution; Sec. 4, 'Methods'; Sec. 5, 'Limitations and next steps'
weaknesses.suggestion: State in the 'Methods' paragraph that the single control for filtering is logistic regression at the same fixed C, and tie the recovery claim to that baseline ('at fixed C'). Use the chance reference the data already supply for selection quality: removing the same number of samples at random has an expected precision equal to Flip and an expected recall equal to Drop, so say this when introducing Prec. and Rec. in Table 1. Add that stronger regularization was not tried to the limitations, and move the sentence on not attributing the gain to removing the right samples next to the accuracy result in Sec. 4.2.

weaknesses.issue: The placement against prior work leaves the contribution unclear. The first contribution presents the filter itself, while the paragraph above says no new method is claimed. The gap in the introduction (other repairs need corruption probabilities or noise rates 'which then have to be estimated') does not separate this work from its closest relatives, since such quantities can be estimated from the noisy data, and confident learning also needs no clean set and no known noise rate. To my knowledge, the confident learning paper itself evaluates the argmax-disagreement rule as one of its variants (the confusion-matrix method); please check the source.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 1, paragraphs 2 and 3 and first contribution; Sec. 2, 'Filtering mislabeled samples'
weaknesses.suggestion: Replace the first contribution with a measurement contribution (what an existing single-learner classification filter removes, recovers and costs for a linear model on clean and noisy labels). In Sec. 2, say exactly which published rule this equals, after verifying it. Rewrite the second paragraph of the introduction around the unknown that the study answers, not around inputs that other methods need.

weaknesses.issue: The most direct measure of whether filtering works, the share of mislabeled samples left in the kept set, is never reported, and the main failure is described but not examined. From results/runs.jsonl (my approximate computation, mean of per-seed ratios), the kept set is about 0.4% and 2% mislabeled on digits at the lower and higher rates, about 2% on breast cancer at the lower rate and about 15% on breast cancer at the higher rate. In that last setting, the two seeds that end near 74% accuracy are also the two with the highest realized noise rate (about 42% against 35 to 38%) and the most residual noise (about 18 to 24% against 8 to 13%). This is a much stronger and more informative result than what the text offers ('Accuracy there varies widely between seeds'; 'Our runs do not show that one causes the other').
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4.1, Table 1; Sec. 4.2, 'Recovery is partial'; Fig. 1c, breast cancer at 40%
weaknesses.suggestion: Add a column to Table 1 with the mislabeled share of the kept set, next to Flip., with recipes from the existing runs. Add two sentences on breast cancer at the higher rate that report the realized noise rate and residual noise of the low and high seeds, worded as an association across five seeds. The space can come from the duplicated figures and the MLP paragraph.

weaknesses.issue: The statistics cannot be checked and their binary use misleads. The text repeatedly says that the seeds do or do not 'establish' a result, but no significance level, p-value or interval appears anywhere. The list of settings that remain below the clean-label reference omits digits at the lower rate, although its mean gap in Table 2 is slightly larger than that on breast cancer at the lower rate, which is listed (the two p-values in the project notes sit just on either side of 0.05). Breast cancer at the lower rate is counted among the settings that win back much of the lost accuracy although the gain itself is not established there, and from the raw runs its per-seed recovered share ranges from below zero to 100%. The test of whether the share exceeds one half has no stated motivation.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4, 'Checks and statistics'; Sec. 4.2, first two paragraphs; abstract; captions of Figs. 1 and 2
weaknesses.suggestion: State the significance level and whether any multiple-comparison correction was applied. Report the paired difference with sd and p-value (or interval) as an extra row in Table 2 or in the Fig. 2 caption. Drop the one-half tests. Describe breast cancer at the lower rate as a higher mean that is unresolved, with an unstable recovered share, in the abstract, contributions and Sec. 4.2. Report both lower-rate gaps to the clean-label reference in the same way.

weaknesses.issue: The paragraph on how heavier noise shifts the drops compares precision across settings whose share of flipped labels doubles. Precision rising on digits therefore does not mean that selection improved: relative to the flipped share it falls. The table values also imply that the share of correct samples discarded grows from the lower to the higher rate on both datasets (roughly 13 to 20% on digits and 7 to 23% on breast cancer, my computation from the recorded drop shares), which is the clearer finding and is not reported.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4.1, 'Heavier noise shifts what is dropped'
weaknesses.suggestion: Report the share of correctly labeled samples that are dropped next to recall, and say that at the higher rate the filter both misses more flips and discards a larger share of the correct samples. Discuss precision only relative to Flip. Also note that Drop exceeds Flip in every noisy row, which states the 'price' directly.

weaknesses.issue: The setup omits the number of classes and features. Digits is a ten-class image task and breast cancer a binary tabular task. This matters for reading symmetric noise: at 40% a binary label carries little information, while in ten classes the wrong labels spread over nine classes. A reader needs this to interpret the one clear weak case and the low MLP accuracy there.
weaknesses.suggestion: Add classes and features for both datasets (with recipes or a cited dataset description), say that digits is the only image dataset, and mention the binary case when discussing the higher rate on breast cancer without presenting it as a proven cause.

weaknesses.issue: In a four-page paper the same results appear two or three times: accuracy in Fig. 1c, Table 2 and Fig. 2, and drop statistics in Fig. 1b and Table 1. The room this takes is what the missing analysis and statistics need.
weaknesses.suggestion: Keep the pipeline in Fig. 1a plus one result panel (for example, move the paired differences of Fig. 2 into the Fig. 1c slot), and shorten the long Fig. 1 caption to match.

weaknesses.issue: Fig. 1c draws bars on an accuracy axis that starts near 55%, so bar length exaggerates the gains. The axis break and the caption note do not remove this effect. The seed dots and sd whiskers are also hard to separate at print size, especially in the clean columns.
weaknesses.suggestion: Remove the panel in favor of the paired-difference plot, or plot means and seed dots without bars on the truncated axis.

weaknesses.issue: The results prose is hard to follow and repeats its caveats. The unresolved gain on breast cancer at the lower rate is stated in the Fig. 1 caption, the Fig. 2 caption, Sec. 4.2 and Sec. 5. 'Recovery is partial' chains several conditional statements about which share exceeds one half. The statement that the advantage is larger at the higher rate than with clean labels compares against a setting where no gain is expected. The sentence on t-tests ('paired between methods, noise rates or two shares from the same run, or compare a share with one half') cannot be parsed on first reading. The third contribution is one long sentence with several exceptions.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4.2; Sec. 4, 'Checks and statistics'; Sec. 1, third contribution; Figs. 1 and 2 captions
weaknesses.suggestion: Give each results paragraph one finding and one pointer, state each caveat once where the result appears, move test details into the statistics row suggested above, and shorten the third contribution.

weaknesses.issue: A full paragraph and a table row go to an untuned MLP that, by the paper's own account, says nothing about filtering. The clean-label section also ends on the MLP rather than on the filter's cost.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4.2, 'The MLP gap does not isolate filtering'; Sec. 4.3; Table 2
weaknesses.suggestion: Reduce this to one or two sentences: unfiltered logistic regression also beats this MLP in every noisy run, so the row is context only. Use the space for the kept-set analysis.

weaknesses.issue: Sec. 4.3 reports small mean differences and a non-significant test without their scale. On breast cancer the whole clean-label difference comes from a single seed, where it amounts to one test sample; the two models have the same test accuracy in the other four seeds.
weaknesses.suggestion: Say this directly. It is more informative than reporting that paired tests cannot distinguish the difference from zero and then noting that this does not show equivalence.

weaknesses.issue: The experimental section includes a sentence about the Scriptorium agent pipeline. It says nothing about the experiments, and the cited software entry carries personal names and a repository link, which may conflict with anonymous review.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4, 'Checks and statistics', first sentence; reference [7]
weaknesses.suggestion: Delete the sentence and the reference from the review version and use the space for the significance level.

weaknesses.issue: Some reproducibility details are missing: the logistic regression penalty and solver (library defaults), the 5000 iteration limit, and the fact that a given seed uses the same train/test split at every noise rate, which the pairing across noise rates relies on. Software versions are not stated.
weaknesses.suggestion: Add one or two sentences: library-default penalty and solver, at most 5000 iterations, and a split shared across noise rates for each seed. Add versions only if they are recorded.

weaknesses.issue: The first discussion paragraph mostly restates the results, and 'Running it did not require knowing whether the labels were wrong' does not convey a clear point. Related work could also cover close neighbors on cross-validation-based sample selection and on linear classifiers under label noise. Several bibliography entries are incomplete.
weaknesses.suggestion: Replace the restatement with what a practitioner should check before using the filter (drop fraction, class count, expected noise level), marked as suggestions from these runs. Consider, after verification, Chen et al. (ICML 2019) on cross-validation-based clean-sample selection and Natarajan et al. (NeurIPS 2013) on learning with noisy labels. Add the missing venues for co-teaching and DivideMix, and give the scikit-learn entry its journal and publication year (it shows 2012 and no venue).

questions: Is the keep rule identical to the confusion-matrix (argmax disagreement) variant evaluated by Northcutt et al.? If it differs, how?

How much of the shortfall on breast cancer at the higher rate comes from mislabeled samples that survive the filter, and how much from correct samples that are discarded? An oracle filter would separate the two.
Would unfiltered logistic regression with a smaller C, fixed in advance, close a large part of the gap under noise?
On the binary dataset, does the filter remove one class much more often than the other? The saved runs record only total drop counts.
Why was one half chosen as the recovery level to test, and was it fixed before the results were seen?
Did logistic regression and the MLP converge in all runs?
